item.research_question: How can an FCC high-entropy alloy achieve both ultrahigh strength and satisfactory ductility simultaneously across ambient to cryogenic temperatures?
item.material_system: Fe49Mn30Co10Cr10N1 (at %) high-entropy alloy (N1), specifically in partially recrystallized (PRX) and fully recrystallized (FRX) states
item.processing_route: Vacuum-induction melting of pure metals and MnN; hot forging at 1200°C; hot rolling at 1050°C (50% reduction); homogenization at 1200°C for 2 hours; cold rolling to 60% reduction; annealing at 700°C (PRX) or 900°C (FRX) for 3 min followed by water quenching
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 298 K and 77 K with a strain rate of 10−3 s−1
key_findings: The N1-PRX material achieved an ultrahigh yield strength of 1836 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 2048 MPa, and uniform elongation of 11.6% at 77 K.
At 298 K, the N1-PRX material exhibited a yield strength of 1170 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1224 MPa, and uniform elongation of 8.2%.
The volume fraction of LCO laths in the RX zone increased from 6% at 4% strain to 10% at 11.6% strain during cryogenic deformation.
The average diameter of LCO domains in RX grains increased from 0.31 nm (initial) to 0.51 nm after deformation at 77 K.
The LCO lath-induced strengthening contribution to yield strength at 77 K was calculated to be approximately 448 MPa (183 MPa from boundaries + 265 MPa inside laths).
The critical stress for mechanical twinning decreased from 421–438 MPa at 298 K to 318–335 MPa at 77 K.
Work-hardening rates fluctuated significantly during cryogenic deformation, with rates jumping above 4 GPa for N1-PRX and 3 GPa for N1-FRX.
The areal fraction of ε-martensite in the NRX zone increased from 0.7% at 1% strain to 6.0% after fracture (11.6% strain).
item.mechanism: The authors propose that interstitial-driven local chemical order (LCO) dynamically evolves during cryogenic deformation, where LCO domains grow from short-range order (SRO) to medium-range order (MRO) within laths formed from planar-slip bands. This evolution increases lattice friction and local stacking fault energy (SFE), which hinders planar slip and promotes frequent dislocation cross-slip. The combined activation of transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP), twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP), and the dynamic refinement of microstructure by evolving LCO laths leads to exceptional work hardening and ductility alongside ultrahigh strength.
item.limitations: The authors state that the assumption of summing various strengthening contributions (solid-solution, SRO, dislocation, grain-boundary, TWIP, TRIP, LCO) may not be accurate for MEAs and HEAs because the matrix is in a 'whole-solute' state without a well-defined solute, and mechanisms may depend on each other.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the LCO-dominated microstructural design concept can be extended to more alloy classes, such as advanced steels and BCC MEAs/HEAs, where LCO can be dynamically regulated to impact mechanical performances.
quotes: Dense laths composed of the multiscaled LCO domains evolve from planar-slip bands that form in the prior thermomechanical processing, contributing to ultrahigh yield strengths over a wide temperature range.
The mean width of the LCO laths is 54 nm, and the mean spacing between the neighboring laths is 349 nm.
The dimension of LCO within the laths increases continuously with deformation, and the evolution of LCO structures from SRO to MRO promotes the activation of cross-slip.
